questions.q: Define "situational irony" and give one specific example from "The Luncheon" where the outcome contradicts the narrator's expectations.
questions.a: Situational irony occurs when the actual outcome of a situation is sharply contrary to what was expected or considered appropriate. In "The Luncheon," the narrator expects a modest, inexpensive meal because the lady claims "I never eat anything for luncheon" and "I never eat more than one thing," but she proceeds to order caviare, salmon, giant asparagus, ice-cream, coffee, and a peach – resulting in a bill that leaves him penniless for the month. A wrong answer (e.g., "the lady was fat at the end") reveals confusion between situational irony and poetic justice or character outcome.

questions.q: Explain how the narrator's statement "I was too young to have learned to say no to a woman" functions as both character revelation and thematic foreshadowing.
questions.a: The statement reveals the narrator's youthful insecurity and internalized gendered power dynamic (he feels socially obligated to comply), while foreshadowing the entire luncheon disaster: his inability to refuse her initial invitation, to question the restaurant choice, or to stop her escalating orders. A wrong answer focusing only on "he was polite" misses the structural role – this admission frames the power imbalance that drives the plot and underscores the theme of performative politeness as a trap.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "unreliable narrator" to the story: Identify two moments where the narrator's description of the lady reveals more about his own biases than her actual character, and explain the effect.
questions.a: (1) "She gave me the impression of having more teeth, white and large and even, than were necessary for any practical purpose" – this hyperbolic, almost grotesque description reflects the narrator's irritation and class anxiety, not objective portraiture. (2) "She was talkative but since she seemed inclined to talk about me I was prepared to be an attentive listener" – he frames her talkativeness as a flaw while positioning himself as virtuous, yet he later admits she "thrust [asparagus] down her throat in large voluptuous mouthfuls" while he "discoursed on the condition of the drama in the Balkans," revealing his own performative intellect. The effect: the reader must read *against* the narrator to see the lady's calculated performance. A wrong answer that takes the narrator's descriptions at face value misses the irony of his self-justification.

questions.q: Analyze how Maugham structures the story's timeline (the luncheon 20 years ago vs. the present encounter at the play) to create a frame narrative that transforms the anecdote into a meditation on revenge and time.
questions.a: The frame opens and closes in the present ("I caught sight of her at the play... Today she weighs twenty-one stone"), sandwiching the past luncheon as a flashback. This structure does three things: (1) It establishes the narrator's retrospective control – he chooses when to tell the story and how to frame it. (2) It delays the "revenge" reveal until the final sentence, making the physical transformation (21 stone) a delayed punchline that recontextualizes the past gluttony as self-destructive. (3) It shifts the tone from financial terror to complacent satisfaction, allowing the narrator to claim "I have had my revenge at last" without active vengeance – time itself enacted it. A wrong answer that treats the frame as mere chronological bookends misses the thematic work of irony and narrative distance.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The lady is the true villain of the story." Defend or refute using textual evidence about power, performance, and consequence.
questions.a: Refute with nuance: The lady is a predator of social ritual, but the narrator is complicit. Evidence for villainy: She exploits his poverty knowingly ("Foyot's is a restaurant at which the French senators eat"), escalates orders despite claiming dietary restraint, and ends by lecturing him on moderation ("Follow my example"). Evidence for complicity: He chooses to attend, never sets boundaries, and performs "hospitable still, but not exactly effusive" – maintaining the charade to preserve his self-image as a gentleman. The story critiques *both* the exploiter and the enabler trapped by class performance. A wrong answer that simply labels her "greedy" or him "weak" fails to analyze the systemic dynamic Maugham exposes.

questions.q: Create a 4-line diary entry from the lady's perspective on the evening of the luncheon, revealing her internal calculation without breaking her performed persona.
questions.a: Sample: "Thursday at Foyot's. The young author – so eager, so *grateful*. I ordered the salmon, the caviare, the asparagus – each 'one thing' a masterpiece of restraint. He paid with trembling fingers; I praised his 'generous spirit.' A perfect luncheon: I dined like a senator, he learned the cost of flattery. Tomorrow I shall write him a charming note." A poor answer writes her as overtly malicious ("I tricked him!") missing the point that her villainy *is* the performance – she likely believes her own rhetoric about "never eating more than one thing."
